blocks.text: Every field develops its own shorthand, and MCP is no exception, host, client, server, tool, capability, session, the words get used constantly and, if you only half know them, they blur together fast. This lesson is a proper glossary, one term at a time, each with a precise definition and a small concrete example, so that from here on every later lesson can use these words without stopping to re-explain them.
1. Host

The host is the application a person actually opens and uses, a chat interface, a code editor, a voice assistant. It owns the overall user experience and decides which MCP servers to connect to on the user's behalf. A host can run several connections at once, each to a different server, for a different purpose.
Example: a desktop AI assistant application is the host. The person sees only that one app, everything described below happens behind it.
1.1 What the Host Is Not

The host is not the AI model itself, and it is not the server. It is the surrounding application, the thing with a window, a chat box, or a command line, that embeds a model and coordinates one or more client connections on the user's behalf.
2. Client

The client is a piece of code living inside the host that speaks MCP on the host's behalf. A client maintains exactly one connection to exactly one server, if the host needs three servers, it runs three separate client instances.
Example: when a host connects to both a file-system server and a GitHub server, it is running two separate clients under the hood, one per connection.
2.1 One Client, One Server, Always

This one-to-one rule is strict and worth memorizing on its own: a single client instance never multiplexes across multiple servers. If that rule is ever broken in an implementation, matching requests to responses correctly becomes far harder, since ids are only guaranteed unique within one connection.
3. Server

A server is a separate program that exposes a specific set of capabilities, tools to call, resources to read, prompts to reuse, over MCP. A server usually knows nothing about the host it is talking to, and often nothing about AI models at all, it just answers requests according to the protocol.
Example: a small program that wraps a company's internal ticketing system and exposes a create_ticket tool is an MCP server, regardless of which host eventually connects to it.
3.1 Servers Do Not Need to Know About AI at All

A server only needs to correctly implement the MCP protocol, it has no idea whether the thing calling it is an AI model, a human running a debug script, or an automated test suite. This separation is exactly why the same server can be reused by completely different hosts and models without any change to the server's own code.
4. Tool

blocks.alt: A server exposes a tool as an action to take

blocks.text: A tool is a callable action a server exposes, something with side effects or that performs work, along with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema describing the arguments it expects. A model decides to call a tool, the client sends that call to the server, and the server executes it.
4.1 Tool Naming Conventions

Tool names are typically short, lower case, and verb-first, read_file, send_email, create_ticket, describing an action rather than a noun. A clear name paired with a clear description matters more than it sounds, since the model relies entirely on that text to decide when the tool is relevant.
5. Resource

blocks.alt: A server exposes a resource as data to read

blocks.text: A resource is read-only, addressable data a server can hand over, a file, a database row, a cached document, identified by a URI. Unlike a tool, reading a resource is not expected to change anything, it simply pulls information into the conversation.
Example: file:///reports/q3-summary.txt is a resource URI a file-system server might expose, letting a host pull that file's text directly into a model's context.
5.1 Resource URIs Look Like This

blocks.text: 6. Prompt

blocks.alt: A server exposes a prompt as a reusable template

blocks.text: A prompt, in MCP terms, is a reusable, parameterized template a server ships with, a pre-written, well-tested way of asking for something that server is especially good at handling. A client can list available prompts and fill in the parameters a specific prompt expects.
6.1 Prompts Are the Least Commonly Used Piece

Of the three things a server can expose, tools, resources, prompts, prompts see the least real-world use today, most servers ship tools and sometimes resources, fewer bother defining reusable prompt templates. Knowing the term matters for reading the specification correctly even where you rarely encounter it in practice.
7. Capability

A capability is a category of feature a client or server declares it supports during the initialize handshake, tools, resources, prompts, and a few others. Declaring capabilities up front means neither side ever has to guess what the other one offers.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","Declared by","Meaning"],"rows":[["tools","Server","This server exposes callable tools"],["resources","Server","This server exposes readable resources"],["sampling","Client","This client can let the server request a model completion"]]}

blocks.text: 7.1 Capabilities Are Exchanged, Never Guessed

Neither a client nor a server should ever assume the other side supports something it did not explicitly declare during initialize. A client that calls resources/list against a server that never declared a resources capability is relying on undefined behavior, well-built clients simply skip that call.
8. Session

A session is the full, stateful conversation between one client and one server, starting at the initialize handshake and lasting until the connection closes. A server is typically stateless between separate sessions, but within a single session it can track things like which capabilities were agreed on and what has already been discovered.
Example: opening a host application and connecting to a file-system server starts one session, closing the app ends it, reopening the app later starts an entirely new session.
8.1 Session State Lives on Both Ends, Not in the Messages

No single message carries the whole session's history, instead, the client and server each separately remember what was agreed on during initialize and what has happened since. This is why closing and reopening a connection always starts a brand new session, that shared memory does not persist across a torn-down transport.
9. Transport

blocks.alt: A client and server communicate over transport

blocks.text: The transport is the raw channel that actually carries MCP messages back and forth, most commonly standard input and output for a locally run server process, or a streaming HTTP connection for a remote one. MCP itself is transport-agnostic, the same JSON-RPC messages work over either.
9.1 Two Common Transports Today

blocks.content: {"headers":["Transport","Server runs"],"rows":[["Stdio","As a local child process of the host"],["Streamable HTTP","As an independent, possibly remote, process"]]}

blocks.text: 10. JSON-RPC

blocks.alt: A message follows the JSON-RPC format

blocks.text: JSON-RPC is the lightweight, pre-existing message format MCP builds directly on top of, a simple JSON structure for requests, responses, and notifications, each carrying a jsonrpc version field and, for requests and responses, a matching id. MCP did not invent this format, it adopted an established one so it did not need to solve message framing from scratch.
10.1 Why JSON-RPC and Not Something Custom

JSON-RPC already had a stable, well-understood specification, a request has a method, a response has a matching id, done. Reusing it let MCP's designers spend their design effort on what actually needed to be new, tools, resources, prompts, capability negotiation, instead of reinventing message framing that other protocols had already solved well.
11. Notification

A notification is a JSON-RPC message with no id and no expected reply, used for one-way information like progress updates or a signal that a list of tools has changed. Because it expects no reply, the sender never blocks waiting on one.
11.1 Notifications Never Get Acknowledged

Because a notification carries no id, there is nothing for the receiving side to reply to, even if it wanted to. This makes notifications a poor fit for anything the sender truly needs confirmation of, they are meant purely for one-way, best-effort signaling like progress updates.
12. Request

A request is a JSON-RPC message that carries a method, optional params, and an id, and always expects exactly one matching response. Every tools/call, tools/list, or initialize message sent is a request.
12.1 The Anatomy of a Request

items: id, a unique value for this connection, used to match the eventual response
method, the name of the operation being called, like tools/call
params, an object holding whatever arguments that method needs

blocks.text: 13. Response

A response is the reply to a specific request, echoing back the same id, and containing either a result on success or an error on failure, never both at once. A response without a matching earlier request id would be meaningless, the id is what ties the two together.
13.1 Success Versus Error, Never Both

A response is one or the other, a result field on success, or an error field on failure, a well-formed response never contains both at once, and a well-behaved implementation should treat a message with both, or neither, as malformed.
14. Putting the Terms Together: A Worked Example

A user opens a host application, which starts a client connected over a stdio transport to a file-system server. The client sends an initialize request, the server responds with its capabilities, and a session is now open.
The client then sends a tools/list request, a request, and gets back a response listing a read_file tool.

When the model decides to use it, the client sends a tools/call request, the server sends back a response containing the file's content, and along the way, if the read takes a while, the server might send a progress notification.

blocks.title: Every word from this lesson, in one sentence
blocks.content: One session between one client and one server, opened over a transport, made of requests, responses, and notifications encoded as JSON-RPC, exchanging capabilities and then using the tools, resources, and prompts those capabilities describe.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes When Using MCP Terminology

items: Using "server" and "host" interchangeably, they are opposite ends of the connection, not synonyms.
Calling every message a request, notifications look almost identical but carry no id and get no response.
Assuming a resource and a tool are the same thing because both come from a server, a resource is read-only data, a tool performs an action.
Forgetting that a capability is declared, not assumed, never rely on a feature the other side did not explicitly advertise.
Confusing a session with a connection, a session is the whole stateful conversation, the transport is just the pipe carrying it.

blocks.text: 16. Practice: Build Your Own Glossary Entry

Pick one term from this lesson and write your own definition in one sentence, without looking back at this page, then write one example sentence using that term correctly in the context of a server you are familiar with, real or invented.
Then swap your definition with a colleague, or reread it a day later, and check whether it still holds up without you needing to add anything back in.
Key Takeaway

Every MCP term traces back to one of two things, a role in the conversation, host, client, server, or a piece of the message format that carries that conversation along, request, response, notification, capability, session, transport, all riding on plain JSON-RPC.

With the vocabulary now locked down precisely, the next lesson, MCP Ecosystem, looks outward at the real-world landscape built on top of these terms, the official SDKs, the community servers, and the client applications that actually speak this protocol today.
